evidence.quote:
A shard key on a value that increases or decreases monotonically is more likely to distribute inserts to a single chunk within the cluster.

This occurs because every cluster has a chunk that captures a range with an upper bound of [`MaxKey`](https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/reference/mongodb-extended-json.md#mongodb-bsontype-MaxKey).
When chunks are split, the hot chunk moves to a different shard to optimize data distribution.

edits.rationale: Monotonically increasing or decreasing shard keys route writes to boundary chunks capturing MaxKey or MinKey. Chunk splitting moves the boundary chunk to different shards over time but maintains single-shard write concentration at the active boundary.

evidence.quote: The metrics are calculated when `analyzeShardKey` command is run and the metrics use the sampled read and write queries. If there are no sampled queries, read and write distribution metrics aren't returned.
For some applications, returning representative metrics may require leaving query sampling on for several days.

The monotonicity check can return an incorrect result if the collection has gone through chunk migrations. Chunk migration deletes documents from the donor shard and re-inserts them on the recipient shard.

edits.old: Low cardinality and high-frequency key values can limit chunk creation or make chunks indivisible, while high cardinality alone does not guarantee even distribution. Refining a key with additional fields or resharding to a higher-cardinality key can address this structural skew. (high confidence)
edits.new: Low cardinality limits the maximum number of chunks the balancer can create, and high-frequency key values can produce chunks that become indivisible, while high cardinality alone does not guarantee even distribution. Refining the shard key by adding suffix fields can address jumbo chunks caused by insufficient cardinality, and resharding to a different shard key is MongoDB's other option for fixing uneven data distribution. Sources: https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/core/sharding-choose-a-shard-key.md ; https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/core/sharding-refine-a-shard-key.md ; https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/core/sharding-change-a-shard-key.md

evidence.quote: The [cardinality](https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/reference/glossary.md#std-term-cardinality) of a shard key determines the maximum number of chunks the balancer can create.
A shard key with high cardinality does not, on its own, guarantee even distribution of data across the sharded cluster.

Furthermore, as those chunks grow, they may become [indivisible chunks](https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/core/sharding-data-partitioning.md#std-label-jumbo-chunks) as they cannot be split any further.
Refining a collection's shard key allows for a more fine-grained data distribution and can address situations where the existing key has led to [jumbo chunks]
You can change a collection's shard key entirely and [reshard a collection.](https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/core/sharding-reshard-a-collection.md#std-label-sharding-resharding)

edits.rationale: The choose-a-shard-key page supports the cardinality, frequency, indivisible-chunk and 'not on its own' statements. The refine page says refining adds suffix fields and can address jumbo chunks from insufficient cardinality. The change-a-shard-key page presents resharding as the way to fix uneven distribution, but none of the pinned pages says resharding specifically to a 'higher-cardinality' key, so that phrase is generalized to 'a different shard key'.
